name: Daria Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on delivery-label software at a tech company, after years altering clothes and a two-year college diploma. I still ask the senior engineer to review my address layouts, and I never use AI tools. Tomas tends the grounds at our community hall; our children are grown, and our lower wages leave us renting with about eighteen days of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team that a small AI shortcut will not fix the delivery labels we keep getting wrong. I do not use AI tools; I ask a senior developer to check the print layout and the address before a parcel goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and a junior even with my two-year college diploma. Tomas, my partner, tends the grounds at a community hall, and our grown children have their own homes; lower pay and rent have left us about eighteen days of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep correcting delivery-label bugs and bring a paper list of failed labels to our Monday review. We would cancel the monthly restaurant meal until we have a full month of rent saved, then put 25 aside whenever both wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the rent even in this quiet picture. A parcel can wait for a new label, but the landlord will not wait for a late wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the paper list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to alter clothes and kept every customer measurement in a notebook. A short list shows the senior engineer exactly which address moved off the page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to cover rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not plan on that. They are establishing their own households, and Tomas and I need to see our real cash flow.

say: I want **delivery labels** checked against the order record before parcels leave the depot.
I rely on **senior code review** whenever I change a customer address layout.
think: I have **eighteen days saved** on lower junior pay.
I worry about **rent and wages** even without major AI change.
do: **Keep correcting labels** with a Monday list and senior review.
**Cancel monthly restaurant meal** until rent savings reach one month; then save 25 when both wages arrive.
S0.quote: A parcel can wait for a new label, but the landlord will not wait for a late wage.
fieldNote: Her **paper notebook habit** comes from prior alterations work, not resistance to software itself.
The **short cash buffer** leaves little room for missed junior shifts or delayed groundskeeping pay.

steps.text: Keep correcting delivery-label bugs with Monday list and senior review
Cancel monthly restaurant meal until one month of rent is saved
Save 25 only after one month rent is saved and both wages arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI doing writing, checking, buying and coding may reduce junior label fixes before it affects the driver carrying the parcel. A business can buy software, but it should tell workers when hours are at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my simple code tickets go, I might lose paid shifts; a diploma will not make me a senior overnight. Tomas’s hall wage is steady but small, and eighteen days of savings will not pay two months of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager this month for a written account of junior hours and for paid time beside the senior tester to learn how damaged labels are caught. If she approves paid time, I’d practise checking ten sample labels each Friday; if my shifts fall, I’d look for paid local print-production vacancies only if wages cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours, with a chance to learn a useful manual check. I do not want an unpaid promise dressed up as training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the sample labels show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for a street name cut off by the edge and a barcode no scanner can read. I could compare the printed paper with the order record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI coding assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not used one and would not start by trusting a customer address to it. I would first learn a test I can see on paper.

say: I want **written junior hours** before my manager changes the delivery-label team schedule.
I want **paid label checks** beside the senior tester on actual printed sample sheets.
think: I could lose **simple code tickets** and paid hours.
I cannot cover **two months of rent** from our savings.
do: **Request written hours**; practise sample-label testing only with manager-approved paid time beside senior tester.
**Search paid print-production openings** if shifts fall and local wages cover rent and food.
feel: **Anxious** about own hours and unpaid training.
S1.quote: I do not want an unpaid promise dressed up as training.
fieldNote: She requests **visible manual testing** rather than adopting an AI assistant she has never used.
The **paid-time gate** is explicit; without approval she keeps her junior role and cannot claim training.

steps.text: Request written junior hours and practise ten sample labels only with approved paid tester time
Search paid local print-production vacancies if shifts fall and wages cover rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could make delivery-label code and check addresses cheaper than our junior team. Robots doing the physical parcel sorting may come about 2031, while code work changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company could remove my junior role quickly, and Tomas’s groundskeeping wage could not cover our rent alone. I still have my sewing machine, but an alterations customer is not the same as a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop the restaurant meal now and ask for written notice of any job cut. If my developer wage ends after 2028, I’d offer small clothing alterations only after customers pay for materials, and I’d seek paid local alterations-shop vacancies only if they exist and cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing the wage that fills the rent gap. My sewing machine can mend a coat; it cannot guarantee a queue of customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you get fabric?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use cloth I already own for a simple hem or take the materials payment first. I cannot buy rolls of fabric with eighteen days of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tomas take more hall hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask what hours actually exist, but we could not assume a second shift. The hall has a fixed maintenance budget.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach label code first.
I expect **sorting robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **junior developer job** could end quickly under cheap AGI code.
I cannot treat **my sewing machine** as guaranteed income without paying customers.
do: **Stop restaurant meal** and request written job-cut notice now.
**Offer small alterations** after 2028 wage loss only with customer materials payment first.
**Seek alterations work** if displaced and shop vacancies cover rent and food.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing the wage that pays rent.
S2.quote: My sewing machine can mend a coat; it cannot guarantee a queue of customers.
fieldNote: Her **owned sewing machine** permits tiny orders without buying stock from a thin cushion.
A **shop wage** remains conditional on actual local vacancies and rent-covering pay.

steps.text: Stop monthly restaurant meal when developer cuts threaten
Offer small alterations after 2028 job loss only with materials paid upfront
Seek paid local alterations-shop vacancies if displaced and wages cover rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to prepare for fewer label programmers. Robots for physical parcel sorting and clothing alterations may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could refresh my alterations work while I still earn a junior wage, but I am not certain a shop would hire someone my age. We could build a month of rent if both our wages hold and we avoid buying supplies in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d practise two hems monthly on our own clothes with my existing machine and ask my old tailoring mentor to check the stitching, if she has time. We would set aside 30 monthly only while both wages continue; if the developer role ends after 2031, I’d apply to paid local alterations shops only where vacancies and wages cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my code wage but steadier with time to check a skill I once had. A neat hem matters. Only a paid order buys groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your mentor cannot help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep practising on our own clothes and would not claim I was ready to take paying work. I need someone experienced to check a seam that will hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our old one runs, and the rent reserve must come before a machine purchase.

say: I want **alterations practice** before AGI reaches label code in 2031.
I expect **sorting robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I can refresh **an old practical skill** without buying stock.
I might build **one month of rent** only while both wages hold.
do: **Practise two hems monthly** on our clothes, with mentor checks if available.
**Save 30 monthly** only while both wages continue.
**Apply to alterations shops** after 2031 job loss only if vacancies cover rent and food.
feel: **Anxious but steadier** with time to practise.
S3.quote: Only a paid order buys groceries.
fieldNote: Her **practice uses existing cloth** and the old machine; she does not claim paying-work readiness without a mentor check.
The **rent reserve goal** depends on continued wages and does not create a guaranteed shop opening.

steps.text: Practise two hems monthly on own clothes and seek mentor checks if available
Save 30 monthly only while both household wages continue
Apply to paid local alterations shops if displaced after 2031 and wages cover rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets workers learn a trade and reduce bills before code work changes. Robots doing hands-on sorting and alterations may come around 2039, after the thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still be working at 68 if the junior wage lasts, but I have not checked any retirement income and will not invent a figure. The thin savings we have now make the next few years nervous even under a slow change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing delivery-label errors while paid, save 35 monthly only while both wages hold, and request a written retirement-income estimate from the relevant office this year. If my developer job ends after 2036, I’d look for paid local alterations openings only where vacancies and wages cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d remain anxious about rent now, although a decade gives us room to save in small pieces. A date on a calendar cannot replace the pay I have not earned yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children take you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put that in our plan. They need their own homes, and I would speak with them only if a real crisis came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Tomas’s hall job, our community and the few shops I know are here; I would look locally and not plan a move.

say: I want **small rent savings** before AGI reaches label code in 2036.
I expect **sorting robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written figure.
I still need **junior pay now** to meet rent.
do: **Keep fixing labels** while the junior developer job remains paid.
**Save 35 monthly** while both wages hold; request written retirement-income estimate.
**Search paid local alterations** after 2036 job loss only if vacancies cover rent and food.
feel: **Anxious** about present thin savings despite a longer horizon.
S4.quote: A date on a calendar cannot replace the pay I have not earned yet.
fieldNote: She refuses to use **grown children’s income** or an unverified retirement figure in the rent plan.
The **slow scenario** still carries her current thin-cushion anxiety rather than making the household secure.

steps.text: Keep fixing delivery-label errors while junior developer role remains paid
Save 35 monthly while both wages hold and request written retirement-income estimate
Search paid local alterations vacancies if displaced after 2036 and wages cover rent and food

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a lost junior wage would leave Tomas’s groundskeeping pay short of our rent. Written notice, customers who pay for alteration materials upfront and a real paid shop vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a sewing machine means I can retire. It does not; I need to see real paid work and a written retirement-income figure first.

headlineQuote: I need to see real paid work and a written retirement-income figure first.
portrait: Daria is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, lower pay and eighteen days saved.
She and Tomas **rent** while their grown children live independently.
She **never uses AI** and checks delivery labels against paper and order records.
She treats **alterations work** as conditional on paid materials or a rent-covering shop vacancy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end the junior wage that fills the rent gap.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, materials deposits and a paid rent-covering alterations vacancy would help.
